newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stock index futures end uneventful day mixed.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stock index futures end uneventful day mixed.

text.p: U.S. stock index futures closed an uneventful session mixed, with June Standard & Poor's 500 ending on a weak note.
"S&Ps needed a catalyst to test the upper end of their recent ranges, but we just didn't get one," one S&P futures trader said.

The result was a choppy, thinly traded session that caught June S&Ps between marginal gains and slim losses. June attempted to retest the session low of 846.00 in the final minutes of trade, as the Dow Jones Industrial Average continued to sell off, traders said.
They said the modest rebound in some technology stocks kept June from testing the pivot point of 835.20 and support at 831.50, which was Friday's pit low.

They also said the constructive closing tone in U.S. T-bond futures also limited downside momentum. The yield on the U.S. cash bond remained below the 7.00 percent level, feeding beliefs that U.S. stocks were a more attractive investment than U.S. government securities, they said.
However, June lacked solid buyers that could have turned the contract up towards the daily and GLOBEX high of 853.90. Traders noted scattered buying in early-morning trade.
At the opening, some floor traders were calling for a retest of the all-time high of 854.70 before midday.
"We were nowhere near resistance today," another trader said later in the day. "There wasn't a whole lot of justification for our overnight high."
Meanwhile, Nikkei futures closed sharply higher. Some floor sources said dealers were beginning to roll June positions into the September contract. June's last trading day is Thursday, June 12.
They also noted a light rolling over of positions into September S&Ps from the June contract.
The last trading day for June S&Ps is Thursday, June 19.

The sharp rise in the U.S. May National Association of Purchasing Management index on manufacturing activity, which was released on Monday morning, pressured U.S. stocks throughout the day, traders said.
NAPM rose to 57.1 in May from April's 54.2, compared with average trade estimates for a decline to 53.9.
May NAPM was the highest since November 1994, heightening concerns that the U.S. manufacturing sector grew at a strong rate in the second quarter.
Last week, both U.S. bond and stock traders were beginning to believe that the rate of U.S. economic growth would slow from the first quarter, traders and analysts said.
Fair value for June S&Ps stood at 1.70 points to cash, with arbitrage buy programs at a premium of 2.90 points and arbitrage sell programs at a premium of 1.00 point.

At the end of pit trade, June S&Ps were off 4.40 points at 846.20, KCBT Value Lines were 3.90 higher at 759.70, NYSE Composites fell 1.30 to 441.50, Nikkeis were up 270 at 20,410, Midcap 400s were 1.60 higher at 281.25, Nasdaq 100s lost 4.00 to 958.75 and Russell 2000s rose 4.10 at 384.70.
